questions.title: What exactly is hyperspherical energy and why does preserving it matter for diffusion model finetuning?
questions.question_body:
In the paper "Controlling Text-to-Image Diffusion by Orthogonal Finetuning" the authors introduce hyperspherical energy (HE) as a measure of pairwise neuron similarity on the unit hypersphere. I understand that HE is computed as 
$$	ext{HE}(W)=	frac{1}{2} rac{n^2-n}{ eta} igg( rac{1}{n}  igg( rac{1}{ eta n}  igg)^{-1} - 	frac{ eta}{2} iggr)$$
but the exact formula is not shown. Why is keeping the HE of a layer unchanged crucial for maintaining the generative/semantic quality of a pre‑trained diffusion model? How does changing neuron angles while preserving HE ensure that high‑level knowledge is not lost?

questions.title: How does orthogonal transformation guarantee preservation of pairwise angles but allow learning new directions?
questions.question_body: Equation (3) in the paper states that if a weight matrix $W$ can be written as $W = R W^0$ with $R^	op R = I$, then the hyperspherical energy of $W$ equals that of $W^0$. Why does this imply that all pairwise cosine similarities between neurons stay identical? Is this property only true for a single layer, or does it extend to deeper networks with multiple layers where the output of one layer becomes the input to another?

questions.title: Why do we need block‑diagonal orthogonal matrices instead of full‑rank ones?
questions.question_body: The paper proposes a block‑diagonal parametrisation for $R$ to reduce parameter count: $R = 	ext{diag}(R_1, R_2, …, R_r)$. What would happen if we used a full‑rank orthogonal matrix ($r=1$)? Would the optimisation steps become noticeably slower, or would it affect convergence? Are there any empirical results comparing these two settings?

questions.title: How is the Cayley transform used to enforce orthogonality during training?
questions.question_body: The authors mention that they parameterise $R$ via the Cayley transform: $R = (I + Q)(I - Q)^{-1}$ where $Q$ is skew‑symmetric. Could someone walk me through how this guarantees $R^	op R = I$? Also, how do you efficiently compute $(I - Q)^{-1}$ in back‑propagation without running into numerical instability?

questions.title: Why isn’t minimizing hyperspherical energy used as a training objective in OFT unlike in Liu et al.'s work?
questions.question_body: The authors say that minimizing HE would destroy pre‑trained semantics, whereas keeping it constant preserves them. Could someone provide an example (perhaps with toy weights) showing that a minimal HE arrangement could merge or remove important features learned during pretraining?

questions.title: $R$ multiplies $W^0$—does this change gradient flow during fine‑tuning?
questions.question_body: "OFT performs finetuning by learning a matrix 𝐑 such that 𝐓=𝑲(ᵒ¹𝑇𝐑)^T oldsymbol{x}". Since 𝐑 is shared across all neurons in a layer, does this reduce parallelism or change how gradients are propagated compared to standard weight updates? How do you implement this efficiently in PyTorch or another DL framework?

questions.title: How are control consistency metrics computed in controllable generation tasks?
questions.question_body: "The paper introduces a control consistency metric based on estimating the control signal from generated images and comparing it with the original input control signal (e.g., IoU for Canny edges). How exactly is this estimation performed? Are external models used? If so, which ones and what are their roles in computing F1 or accuracy scores?

questions.title: Can we combine OFT with LoRA-like low‑rank updates for added flexibility?
questions.question_body: "OFT restricts updates to orthogonal transformations, whereas LoRA uses low‑rank additive updates. Would mixing both strategies—an orthogonal multiplicative part plus a low‑rank additive part—help capture both angle and magnitude changes while still preserving HE approximately? Has such hybrid been empirically tested?

questions.title: Why does OFT converge faster than LoRA or fine‑tuning from scratch in diffusion models?
questions.question_body: "The authors claim two reasons: (1) neuron directions are key for semantics, and (2) optimisation occurs on a smooth hypersphere manifold. Could someone elaborate on #2? What ab initio properties of an orthogonally constrained manifold lead to smoother loss landscapes compared to unconstrained weight optimisation?

questions.title: "Cayley transform requires matrix inversion – how scalable is OFT for very high dimensional layers such as those in large transformers?

"In practice, some layers have dimensions >10k. Performing $(I-Q)^{-1}$ per update seems expensive. Besides block‐diagonal tricks mentioned, are there other ways (e.g., series expansion approximation, QR factorisation) to enforce orthogonality efficiently? Any discussion on computational overhead relative to mainstream finetuning methods?
